newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists open fire on defence scheme.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists open fire on defence scheme.

text.p: The probable next chairman of the French National Assembly's defence committee called on Friday for a review of controversial plans to take in young people for five days to assess their suitability for the military and lecture them on patriotism.
"The system would be expensive, useless, an imposition on our youth and would further disorganise our armed forces," said former defence minister Paul Quiles, a Socialist.
He said the "Citizens' Meetings" scheme would cost at least two billion francs ($350 million) "which would be better employed elsewhere in the defence budget".

Quiles has been officially chosen as the Socialist candidate in next week's vote for chairman of the defence committee, a job he should clinch easily thanks to his party's predominance in parliament after the general election in May and June.
"It is obvious that this idea must be reviewed," Quiles told LCI television. The still-untested scheme is the brainchild of former conservative defence minister Charles Millon.

Millon said the scheme, which was to begin this month but has been postponed, would have maintained a link between the population and the armed forces once France's armies became entirely professional by 2002.

France has had compulsory military service for men off and on for about 200 years, but President Jacques Chirac decided last year to phase it out as inefficient and because it was unpopular among young people.

Under the new system young men, and later young women as well, would be called to military centres in groups of several hundred, to undergo medical checks in case national service was to be reinstituted, and to be lectured on civic values.
The hierarchy of the armed forces were initially outraged at the idea, privately branding it a useless election gimmick without military value that would draw on defence budgets and personnel.
There has since been a change of heart and the military now sees the meetings as an opportunity to recruit youths for the professional army.
But Socialist Party defence experts have opposed the project throughout, though they agree on the need to end conscription and make the armed forces entirely professional.
